### 6.4.4 Doctrinal Construction of Law & The Reconstruction of Individual Sovereignty: Toward Equitable Regulatory Harmonization

Facing the complex threats of this digital sovereignty era, the doctrinal reconstruction of civil and public law is an urgent imperative. Within the framework of Indonesian substantive civil law—specifically referring to Article 1320 in conjunction with Article 1328 of the Indonesian Civil Code (*Burgerlijk Wetboek*)—a binding agreement requires free consent untainted by mistake (*dwaling*), fraud (*bedrog*), or duress (*bedreiging* / *undue influence*) (Subekti, 2014). 

Hitherto, this doctrine has been rigidly applied to physical interpersonal interactions. However, if a technology corporation employs AI-driven subliminal manipulation and the illusion of artificial intimacy to compel consent or fraudulently extract personal data, such a defect of will must be legally recognized as a form of systemic fraud and undue algorithmic influence (Balkin, 2016). Consequently, any end-user license agreements (*EULA*) or data collection consents obtained through affective manipulation must be declared null and void (*batal demi hukum*), as they violate the subjective and objective requirements for a valid contract.

At the sectoral and international regulatory levels, this legal construction must be aligned with the highest standards of global protection, such as the EU AI Act 2024 (specifically Article 5, which explicitly prohibits manipulative or deceptive practices that materially distort human behavior) and the Indonesian Personal Data Protection Act (Law No. 27/2022) (Veale & Borgesius, 2021; Sinta Dewi, 2023). Nevertheless, this harmonization must not stop at the passive adoption of foreign legal texts; it must be incorporated into national legal sovereignty by expanding the scope of personal data protection to encompass psychographic and cognitive dimensions (Greenleaf, 2020). 

The state must designate AI systems that function as affective persuasion agents, synthetic emotional advisors, or behavioral manipulators as high-risk AI systems. These systems must be subjected to mandatory independent audits, fundamental rights impact assessments, and rigorous human-in-the-loop oversight before being permitted to operate within national jurisdiction (Veale et al., 2018).

The reconstruction of individual sovereignty in the digital era also demands a shift from notice-and-consent protection doctrines toward privacy and safety by design and substantive justice (Cavoukian, 2009; Solove, 2013). Consumers and data subjects should no longer bear the burden of reading thousands of words of terms-of-service documents intentionally crafted to obscure exploitative clauses. 

Instead, the law must impose a fiduciary duty upon AI service providers to act in the best interests of users, prohibit any form of interface design that exploits emotional or cognitive vulnerabilities, and grant broad standing for victims of algorithmic manipulation to sue for proportional damages (Balkin, 2020). A sovereign state is one capable of ensuring that its citizens are not subjugated by rows of mathematical code masquerading as companions or advisors.

As a final synthesis, the harmonization of national regulations and global ethical standards in the era of digital sovereignty is not merely a technical matter of adjusting statutory articles; it is an existential struggle to preserve human dignity itself (Habermas, 2001).
